prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Database column specification for orders table (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 9 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Column" · longest unbreakable word 137px · one-line width 137px
  col 2: header "Type" · longest unbreakable word 99px · one-line width 210px
  col 3: header "Nullable" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 59px
  col 4: header "Default" · longest unbreakable word 161px · one-line width 161px
  col 5: header "Comment" · longest unbreakable word 93px · one-line width 577px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 792px (the dashed pink box). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 791px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 792px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"A database schema reference for the orders table, used by developers/DBAs to verify column names, types, nullability, defaults, and meaning before querying or migrating.","reading":"Readers scan down the Column list to locate a field, then move horizontally across Type, Nullable, and Default to confirm its contract; the Comment is read last as explanation. Comparison happens primarily within columns, so identifiers and technical tokens should remain stable and easy to align.","groups":["Column, Type, Nullable, Default — the machine-readable schema contract, read together row by row","Comment — free-text human annotation, secondary to the schema facts and naturally wrappable"],"keep_intact":["order_id","customer_id","order_reference","status","total_amount_cents","currency_code","placed_at","cancelled_at","BIGINT UNSIGNED","VARCHAR(32)","VARCHAR(24)","INTEGER","CHAR(3)","TIMESTAMP","CURRENT_TIMESTAMP","NULL","'pending'","'USD'","YES/NO values"],"may_wrap":["Comment prose","Type phrases between words, such as TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE","Longer comments can increase row height without harming the row’s meaning"]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[165,195,80,182,169],"idea":"Balanced scan: give the schema-fact columns enough room to stay readable while allowing comments to wrap to a moderate height."},{"name":"B","widths":[158,140,80,182,231],"idea":"Comment-first: compress the Type column to its unbreakable tokens and spend the reclaimed width on readable comment prose."},{"name":"C","widths":[160,231,80,182,138],"idea":"Schema-first: preserve every Type value on one line and keep defaults intact, accepting narrow, heavily wrapped comments as secondary annotation."}]}
